clinicalPearls: Caused by Bartonella bacilliformis and transmitted by nocturnal female Lutzomyia sandflies in the Andean valleys of Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.
It is a biphasic illness: an acute haemolytic phase (Oroya fever) and a chronic cutaneous phase (verruga peruana), which may be separated by weeks to months.
Oroya fever is a severe febrile haemolytic anaemia caused by massive erythrocyte invasion, with high mortality if untreated.
Immune suppression during the acute phase predisposes to opportunistic superinfection, classically with Salmonella, so empirical antibiotic choice should cover it.
Verruga peruana consists of reddish angiomatous skin nodules that may ulcerate and bleed, with histology showing vascular endothelial proliferation.
A Giemsa-stained blood film may reveal intraerythrocytic organisms during the acute phase.
Named after Daniel Alcides Carrion, who self-inoculated verruga material and died of Oroya fever, proving the two phases were one disease.
Consider the diagnosis in a febrile, anaemic traveller returning from endemic Andean regions.
reference.pathophysiology: Bartonella bacilliformis is a small motile Gram-negative bacillus inoculated into the skin by the bite of infected female Lutzomyia sandflies. The organism shows a striking tropism for two cell types: erythrocytes and vascular endothelium. In the acute phase (Oroya fever), bacteria adhere to and invade red cells, deforming their membranes and marking them for premature destruction in the spleen, producing a profound haemolytic anaemia; the accompanying reticuloendothelial and immune impairment predisposes to secondary infection, particularly by Salmonella and other intracellular pathogens. If the patient survives, the chronic eruptive phase (verruga peruana) develops, in which bacterial products stimulate marked endothelial cell proliferation and neovascularisation, generating the characteristic angiomatous cutaneous nodules. Prolonged asymptomatic bacteraemia in survivors provides a human reservoir that sustains ongoing sandfly-borne transmission.
additionalDifferentials: Malaria in a febrile returning traveller with haemolysis
Other causes of acute haemolytic anaemia or sepsis
Enteric (typhoid) fever and other Salmonella infection
Bacillary angiomatosis due to Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana (verruga phase)
Pyogenic granuloma and cutaneous haemangioma (verruga phase)
additionalInvestigations: Giemsa-stained thin and thick blood films looking for intraerythrocytic organisms
Blood cultures for Bartonella and to detect Salmonella co-infection
Serology such as indirect immunofluorescence and Bartonella-specific PCR
Full blood count, reticulocyte count and markers of haemolysis
Skin biopsy and histology of verruga lesions, including Warthin-Starry staining
Malaria films and other parasite screening in a returning traveller
redFlags: Rapidly worsening anaemia with haemodynamic compromise during the acute phase
Features of secondary sepsis such as Salmonella infection, including altered mental state or deterioration despite treatment
Neurological involvement (confusion, seizures or focal signs) suggesting neurobartonellosis
Pregnancy, which carries high maternal and fetal mortality
Profuse bleeding from ulcerated verruga lesions
reference.prognosis: Untreated Oroya fever carries very high mortality, largely from anaemia and secondary infection, but it responds well to prompt antibiotic therapy; the verruga peruana phase is generally benign and self-limiting, though lesions may persist for months.
pitfalls: Failing to cover Salmonella and other opportunistic pathogens when treating the acute phase.
Not considering the diagnosis outside classic endemic foci as transmission zones extend.
Mistaking verruga peruana for Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis or pyogenic granuloma.
Missing concurrent malaria in a febrile returning traveller.
Under-recognising the danger of infection in pregnancy.
management: Prompt antimicrobial therapy for Oroya fever, traditionally chloramphenicol (which also covers Salmonella) or a fluoroquinolone, with a beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone in severe disease
Antibiotic treatment of the verruga peruana phase with azithromycin or rifampicin
Empirical cover for opportunistic Salmonella and other superinfection during the immunosuppressed acute phase
Blood transfusion and supportive care for the profound haemolytic anaemia of the acute phase
Monitoring of haemolysis markers, blood counts and for secondary infection during recovery
Vector avoidance and sandfly control with insecticide-treated nets and repellents to prevent transmission
Referral to infectious diseases or tropical medicine, with attention to endemic Andean exposure
